content.comment_body: Hello experts, I need to connect my [product_name] module to a [product_name] operator panel, but they are separated by two bulkheads. My available space allows only a very short cable run (3-5 cm) inside the first enclosure, and storing excess cable is not possible. As a result, I intend to make custom cables. Is there any available cable wiring diagram for connecting the [product_name] module to the [product_name] panel? Are the serial port connectors for both units sold separately, and what type of power connector does the panel use? Additionally, where can these components be purchased in the UK? Thanks in advance.
PIN 1 = 3.3V Power Supply, PIN 3 = RS485 A, PIN 5 = Ground, PIN 8 = RS485 B. Hope this information helps. manual no=[article_no]

Hi [user_name], I'm not sure which series of [product_name] you are referring to. Typically, the connection cable for the [product_name] operator panel comes included with the panel itself. Different module versions, like [product_name] [article_no], may be supported.

Hello [user_name], You can extend the [product_name] operator panel interface cable by up to 7.5 meters using a standard 1-to-1 serial extension cable with male and female Sub-D 9-pin connectors. With the instructions from the package insert, you could make your own cable with only four conductors, using a well-shielded cable for best results. [company_name] showcased this solution at a trade fair in Frankfurt in 2010. Some users have reportedly extended cables up to 100 meters, but [company_name] does not guarantee performance at that length due to potential signal noise, especially around electrically noisy equipment. Be aware that opto-isolating electronics are built into the connector on the operator panel's interface cable, drawing 3.3V DC supply from the panel, not the module—longer distances can reduce this supply. Hopefully this helps get your system running!

Thanks for the feedback so far. Maybe my original description was unclear, as I haven't found the exact solution yet: 1) The standard cable is too long for my use and its connector shell is too large to fit the enclosure, so I need a smaller connector; 2) I plan to attach a new connector to the shortened cable to pass through the first bulkhead; 3) Then, I'll run a separate cable from this connector through the second bulkhead to the operator panel. I know the serial connector is a 9-pin D type, but what's the power connector?

Hi [user_name], Now I understand your situation! Some users have cut off the Sub-D 9-pin end of the operator panel's interface cable to make it shorter. I am unsure of the exact color mapping, but you can verify the connections with a multimeter after cutting and stripping the cable. Attached is an image showing one user's approach. This method allows the cable to be run through a small hole in the enclosure using a rubber grommet. Hope this clarifies things—note that modifying the cable will void its warranty, though hopefully not the warranty for the module or operator panel itself!

Regarding the power connector: I don't own the operator panel myself, but the power connector resembles a typical phoenix contact type, featuring two holes with tightening screws. You should be able to connect the power cable directly and fit the connector easily, especially if you can fit the 9-pin Sub-D connector (without its cover). I believe the connector is included in the product delivery. For the data cable, just cut it to length, route it appropriately, attach a compact 9-pin Sub-D connector, and solder the connections. Power cable installation can follow standard procedure. Note: The panel's power supply can be 12V DC or 24V AC/DC.

Hello [user_name], Regarding the power supply plug: It's a standard product by Molex—available from electronic component suppliers or catalog vendors such as RS Components. The advantage of the operator panel’s power input is that it isn’t polarized; you can connect wires either way. It accepts a broad input range: 12V DC, 24V AC, or 24V DC. This versatility should simplify your setup. Hope your project goes smoothly!

Thanks everyone. Your input is valuable. I'll receive my operator panel tomorrow. I hoped it could be used without extra casing, but with a Molex power connector, it looks like I’ll need to house it for safety. Is there a mechanical drawing for the panel’s serial cable? I need to know how much extra space to allocate to the left side of the module.

Hi [user_name], I hope you enjoy your new operator panel! It will include the interface cable and the Molex power connector. [company_name] chose to supply power to the interface plug via the operator panel, so necessary components didn’t need to be added to the modules and space could be saved. Therefore, you'll need to run power directly to the panel. About space: The interface plug takes up 1TE (roughly the width of a mini circuit breaker). I don’t have a technical drawing, but there's a photo attached from a trade fair in Frankfurt. A cover for the interface plug is available now, which makes installation neater and more secure. It also lets you attach a DIN rail clamp for stability. A clamp on its own is less effective. Hope this is helpful.

Have to admit, this setup looks much improved compared to the original. Thanks for sharing this info. I’ll look into these options when building my control cabinet. Hopefully [company_name] will make a similar module for GSM modems in the future—there’s a perfectionist inside me!

Thanks again for everyone's help. My operator panel arrived today. As expected, the connector for the left side of the module is too large for the available space. However, I may be able to shift the module 10mm to the right by reorganizing and remounting other components in the enclosure (no DIN rail option here). Is the interface cable available separately from the panel? I might need to supply the enclosure with the cable attached but without the panel itself...

analysis.insight_summary: Users encounter physical installation challenges when connecting the [product_name] operator panel to the [product_name] module, including space limitations and oversized cable connectors. The supplied cables are often too long and connectors too bulky, necessitating custom solutions. There is a lack of comprehensive documentation—particularly wiring diagrams and mechanical drawings—which complicates unique installations. Power connector types and supply options also cause some confusion. Overall, the hardware is functional, but lacks flexibility in diverse installation scenarios.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect clear documentation, including wiring diagrams and mechanical drawings, more compact connectors, and flexible installation choices. They also hope for official support for custom cable configurations to accommodate tight spaces and complex setups.
